strengths: Addresses a well-known and practically important limitation of Equilibrium Propagation (EP): slow convergence and instability, which has hindered its adoption despite biological plausibility advantages.

The core technical idea—scaling down feedback strength (rather than forward weights) to control spectral radius and accelerate convergence—is simple, clearly motivated by RNN dynamics theory, and empirically effective, yielding order-of-magnitude speedups over prototypical EP (P-EP) while approaching BP-level accuracy.

Combining residual/skip connections with EP to counteract vanishing gradients in deep (up to 10-hidden-layer) RNNs is a useful extension, and the paper demonstrates it restores much of the lost accuracy (Table 2), including for asymmetric arbitrary-graph-topology networks.

Reasonably thorough empirical study: sweeps over feedforward/feedback scaling coefficients, network depth, symmetric vs. asymmetric connections, convolutional architecture, and comparison against P-EP, BP, and feedback alignment (FA) baselines.
Inclusion of dynamical systems diagnostics (maximum Lyapunov exponent / finite-time MLE) to characterize convergence behavior adds some rigor beyond just accuracy numbers.

Appendix provides a theoretical derivation connecting EP, local representation alignment (LRA), and BP under the weak-feedback/weak-supervision limit, which is a nice unifying contribution alongside the empirical work.
Reasonably well-grounded biological motivation connecting feedback regulation and residual/long-range connectivity to known cortical circuit properties.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to MNIST and FMNIST, which are small, simple datasets; despite claims in the abstract about applicability to 'large-scale networks that underpin AI,' no experiments on more realistic benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-scale, or non-vision tasks) are provided, so scalability claims are not well substantiated.

The central mechanism (scaling spectral radius/feedback strength to control RNN convergence) is a fairly direct application of well-established ideas from reservoir computing and echo-state network literature (cited in Background), and closely related to concurrent work (adjoint propagation, Liu et al. 2025) that the authors acknowledge achieves 'similar' speed and accuracy—raising questions about the degree of novelty.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different optimizers, batch sizes, and learning-rate schedules between P-EP and the proposed method (e.g., batch size 20 vs. 500, SGD vs. Adam), which confounds the reported training-time speedups; a more controlled ablation isolating the effect of feedback scaling alone (holding other training hyperparameters fixed) would strengthen the claims.

The manuscript's clarity suffers from numerous formatting/OCR-type issues and missing values in text (e.g., garbled equations, blank code repository link), suggesting the submission was not fully polished; some claims (e.g., 'weak feedback contributes to biological hallucinations') are speculative and not substantiated by any evidence or citation-backed argument.
The theoretical equivalence proof (EP ≈ LRA ≈ BP at infinitesimal inference limit) largely follows and extends prior work (Millidge et al. 2023) rather than introducing fundamentally new theory.

Limited analysis of failure modes or computational overhead trade-offs when using residual connections in very deep networks beyond 10 layers, and no wall-clock time comparisons are given for the deeper (5/10-layer) experiments in Table 2 as they are for Table 1.
No code repository was actually provided despite a 'Code availability' section, limiting reproducibility verification at review time.

strengths: Identifies a concrete and practical bottleneck in Equilibrium Propagation (slow convergence/instability) and proposes a simple, low-overhead fix (feedback scaling) that yields large empirical speedups (orders of magnitude) while retaining accuracy comparable to BP on MNIST/CIFAR-10 and convolutional benchmarks.

Extensive supporting analysis connecting the feedback-scaling intervention to dynamical-systems quantities (spectral radius, finite-time Lyapunov exponent, convergence time), giving a plausible mechanistic explanation for why down-scaling feedback speeds convergence.

Residual/skip connections and arbitrary graph topologies are shown via ablations to meaningfully alleviate vanishing gradients in deep (10–20 layer) RNNs trained with EP, a previously unaddressed limitation.
Theoretical appendix relating EP under weak feedback/weak supervision to LRA and BP is a nice unifying analysis that supports the empirical findings.

Comprehensive set of ablations, robustness-to-noise experiments, and frozen-layer control experiments add credibility that learning in lower layers is genuinely functional, not just relying on a large final readout.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: code and notebooks provided, detailed hyperparameter tables in appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: scaling feedback strength/spectral radius to control RNN dynamics is a well-known technique (echo-state networks, reservoir computing), and the core contribution is largely an empirical tuning of this existing idea within EP rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The approach essentially pushes EP into a regime where the RNN behaves almost like a feedforward network (as the authors themselves acknowledge in the discussion and appendix C), which raises the question of how much of the claimed 'EP' benefit is retained versus effectively reducing to BP/LRA with extra overhead; this weakens the central motivating claim that this advances genuinely recurrent, brain-like EP dynamics.

Evaluation is limited to MNIST and small/shallow CNNs on CIFAR-10; no results on larger-scale or more realistic architectures/datasets, and the paper explicitly notes an unresolved, non-trivial accuracy gap versus BP on CIFAR-10 with deep fully-connected networks, limiting evidence of practical scalability.

Hyperparameters (feedback scaling ranges, connection probability for AGT, residual topology) are tuned empirically per depth without a principled or automated method to select them, undermining claims of practicality for arbitrary architectures.

Comparisons to more recent, stronger EP variants (e.g., Laborieux & Zenke 2024's Jacobian homeostasis method, which also targets asymmetric/faster EP) are largely qualitative/discussion-level rather than direct empirical comparisons, making it hard to assess relative merit against the current state of the art.

The 10-hidden-layer asymmetric RNN with residual/AGT connections still underperforms both BP and FA substantially on CIFAR-10 (14% gap), and the explanation given is speculative, suggesting the method's benefits are fragile for asymmetric/random-feedback settings which are arguably more biologically realistic.

Some presentation issues: dense notation and algorithm blocks (e.g., Algorithm S3) are hard to parse, and important architectural choices (e.g., why particular residual connections in Figure 3a) lack justification beyond loose analogy to cortical connectivity.
The claimed extension to hardware/neuromorphic implementations is speculative and not empirically demonstrated; all experiments are run on GPUs with standard float32/64 arithmetic.
